docs.title: Database
docs.text: All data lives in one Postgres database. The schema and the queries are written in SQL; the Go code that uses them is described in Persistence layer.

docs.title: Postgres only
docs.text: Noosphere supports exactly one database. Supporting several makes sense for software that other people deploy on the database they already run. Noosphere has one deployment, so it uses Postgres features directly instead of the common subset of several databases: uuidv7() IDs, jsonb columns, IS NFC NORMALIZED checks and transactional schema changes. All SQL stays in db/ and internal/db, so the choice would be contained if it ever changed.

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text: Schema changes are numbered SQL files in db/migrations, applied in order by goose. Each file has an Up part and a Down part that undoes it. A migration that has been applied is never edited; a later change gets a new file. goose runs each migration in a transaction, and Postgres can roll back schema changes, so a failed migration leaves no half-applied schema.

docs.title: Queries
docs.text: SQL queries live in db/queries, and sqlc turns each one into a Go function with typed parameters and results. The SQL stays readable and is checked against the real schema, and Go gets compile-time types without an ORM.

docs.title: IDs and flexible data
docs.text:
Primary keys are UUIDv7 values generated by Postgres. They are unique without coordination and start with a timestamp, so new rows are inserted in order and indexes stay compact.

Data whose shape varies is stored as jsonb: an identity's traits, and each credential's config, whose shape depends on the credential type.

docs.title: Rules in the database
docs.text:
Constraints in the schema enforce the rules that must never be broken, whatever code path writes the row:

  • an identifier is unique per credential type (UNIQUE (type, identifier));
  • an identifier belongs to a credential of the same type (a foreign key on (credential_id, type));
  • a stored identifier is already normalized: lowercase, trimmed, in Unicode NFC form, and not empty (a CHECK constraint).

Go does the full normalization with PRECIS before writing; the CHECK is a safety net that catches any path that skipped it.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Noosphere is a single Go server backed by one Postgres database. It is built one user journey at a time, so the code only contains what the journeys so far need.

docs.title: Stack
docs.text: Part Choice Language Go Database Postgres 18, run locally with Docker Compose Migrations goose, plain SQL files Queries sqlc, which generates typed Go functions from SQL Database driver pgx with its connection pool HTTP routing chi, on top of the standard net/http handlers Pages Server-rendered with html/template (see Web) Password hashing Argon2id from golang.org/x/crypto/argon2 (see Password hashing) Logging log/slog from the standard library Tests Ginkgo and Gomega (see Testing) CI GitHub Actions: make check against a Postgres 18 service on every push and pull request

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
cmd/noosphere/          the server binary: reads settings, builds the logger, the database pool and the web server
internal/web/           HTTP: routes, middleware, handlers, templates and static files
internal/db/            storage: generated query code plus hand-written transactions
internal/identifier/    normalization of login identifiers such as emails
internal/password/      password rules and hashing
internal/pwned/         breached password check against the Pwned Passwords API
internal/logging/       builds the logger from its format and level
internal/dbtest/        test-only: a migrated database per test package
db/migrations/          schema changes, applied in order
db/queries/             the SQL that sqlc turns into Go
db/init/                one-time setup for a new database container (creates noosphere_test, the database TEST_DATABASE_URL names)

Each package has one job, and only cmd/noosphere reads environment variables; the other packages receive their settings as arguments. Code outside internal/db never writes SQL and never sees a Postgres error code: internal/db turns those into plain Go errors such as ErrIdentifierTaken.

docs.title: Everyday commands
docs.text:
The Makefile wraps the common tasks:

Command Does make db-up Starts Postgres and waits until it is ready make migrate-up Applies new migrations to the development database make generate Regenerates the Go query code after a change in db/queries or db/migrations make run Runs the server on http://localhost:8080 against the development database make test Runs all tests; each test package gets its own database on the local Postgres make test-v The same tests through the Ginkgo runner, in random order, printing every spec; extra flags go in ARGS make check Formatting check, go vet, then tests; run before committing

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The server reads its settings from environment variables at startup and stops if one is invalid.

Variable Default Meaning DATABASE_URL none, required Postgres connection string ADDR :8080 Address the server listens on COOKIE_SECURE true Mark cookies Secure (HTTPS only); make run sets false for local HTTP LOG_FORMAT text text or json LOG_LEVEL info debug, info, warn or error PASSWORD_CONTEXT_CHECK true Reject new passwords that are the email, the user's name or the site's name; make run sets false PWNED_PASSWORDS_CHECK true Reject new passwords seen in data breaches, using the Pwned Passwords API; make run sets false PWNED_PASSWORDS_URL https://api.pwnedpasswords.com The API to ask, for example a self-hosted mirror PWNED_PASSWORDS_TIMEOUT 2s How long to wait for an answer before accepting the password anyway

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Every component gets the logger from main instead of using a global one. Log lines are structured: a short message plus key/value pairs, such as flow_id. go vet rejects a key without a value.

Each HTTP request gets a random request_id, stored in its context, returned in the X-Request-ID response header, and included in every line the request logs. After the handler finishes, the access log writes one request line with the method, path, status and duration:

level=INFO msg="registration flow created" request_id=B73V2TUNDMX76PUNOT6AAGWSKY flow_id=01a15cb4-e13c-700a-aad5-2de34f8a9038
level=INFO msg=request request_id=B73V2TUNDMX76PUNOT6AAGWSKY method=GET path=/registration status=303 duration=6.45475ms

A sign-up attempt spans several requests, so it is followed by its flow_id. Secrets (CSRF tokens, passwords, connection strings) and email addresses are never logged, and the access log records the path without the query string.

docs.title: Persistence layer
docs.text: internal/db is the only Go package that talks to Postgres. The rest of the code calls its functions with Go values and gets Go values and Go errors back, never SQL or Postgres error codes.

docs.title: Generated and hand-written code
docs.text:
The package mixes two kinds of code:

  • Generated by sqlc: one Go function per query in db/queries (such as CreateIdentity), a struct per table, and the Queries type that runs them. These files start with Code generated by sqlc. DO NOT EDIT. and are rebuilt with make generate.
  • Hand-written: the Go types that columns map to (types.go), error handling (errors.go), and operations that need several queries in one transaction, such as sign-up (signup.go).

docs.title: Typed values
docs.text: Callers work with Go types, not raw database values. Traits is the identity's profile stored in a jsonb column, CredentialType is the kind of credential (CredentialTypePassword), and PasswordConfig is a password credential's stored config. Turning a struct into JSON for a jsonb column happens inside internal/db, so callers never build JSON by hand.

docs.title: Connections
docs.text:
The server opens one pgx connection pool at startup and pings the database once, because the pool only connects when it is first used and a wrong address should stop the server immediately rather than fail the first request.

The generated Queries runs on anything that can execute SQL: the pool, a single connection or a transaction. The same query functions are used inside and outside transactions.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
An operation that writes several rows runs in one transaction, so it either completes or leaves nothing behind. Sign-up inserts an identity, its credential and the credential's identifier; if the identifier is taken, the identity and credential are rolled back too.

These functions accept anything with a Begin method. The server passes the pool, which starts a transaction. Tests pass their own transaction, on which Begin starts a savepoint, so the operation commits or rolls back inside the test's transaction and the test can still roll everything back at the end.

docs.title: Input at the boundary
docs.text: Values that must follow a rule before they are stored are fixed or rejected here, before the transaction starts. Login identifiers are normalized with PRECIS; an identifier that cannot be normalized returns ErrInvalidIdentifier.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
When Postgres rejects a write, internal/db checks the error code and the name of the constraint that fired, and returns a plain Go error:

Postgres reports Caller receives unique violation on (type, identifier) ErrIdentifierTaken identifier fails normalization (before any SQL runs) ErrInvalidIdentifier

Callers test with errors.Is. The original cause stays wrapped inside, so logs still show what happened. Checking the constraint name matters: a table can have several unique constraints, and only one of them means "this email is already registered".

docs.title: No repository interface
docs.text: Callers use the package's functions directly; there is no interface in front of them and no in-memory fake. The behavior worth testing here, such as constraints, transactions and error mapping, only exists in a real database, so tests run against Postgres (see Testing).

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Tests run against a real Postgres database, and each test layer proves a different thing.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
Layer Tests Example Unit Pure functions, no database or network identifier.Normalize maps Test@Example.com to test@example.com Database Queries, transactions and constraints against real Postgres a second sign-up with the same email returns ErrIdentifierTaken HTTP Handlers through real requests with httptest and a cookie jar POST /registration with a valid form creates the account and redirects to the account-created page End-to-end The built server, driven like a user would sign up, then log in

The database is never mocked. Constraints, transactions and error codes are exactly the behavior worth testing, and a mock would only repeat what the test author already assumed.

docs.title: Isolation
docs.text:
Tests that share a database can see each other's rows. A test that expects one identity finds two, or a sign-up fails with "email already taken" because another test registered the same address a moment earlier. Isolation means every test starts from a known state, no matter what else is running.

There are two places where tests can meet: between test packages, and between tests inside one package.

docs.title: Between packages: a database per package
docs.text:
go test ./... builds each package into its own test binary and runs those binaries in parallel, as many at once as the -p flag allows, which defaults to the number of CPUs (go help build). Two packages that use the same database therefore run at the same time.

That broke when internal/db and internal/web shared one test database. A plain go test ./... failed on its first run:

FAIL! -- 10 Passed | 12 Failed | 0 Pending | 0 Skipped
FAIL    github.com/Tianbo-Qiu/noosphere/internal/db 0.251s

The web tests had committed test@example.com, so a database test inserting the same address hit the unique constraint, and a database test counting identities saw the web tests' rows. The next 40 runs passed: a race like this fails only when the timing lines up, which is what makes it dangerous.

The options:

Option How Why not, or why Run packages one at a time go test -p 1 ./... -p also limits compiling, so builds lose their parallelism; a proposal to separate the two is still open (golang/go#61318). It only protects runs that pass the flag, not an editor or a plain go test. A shared database with a lock Each package takes a Postgres advisory lock for its whole run Works, but packages still wait for each other, and every package must remember to take the lock A database per package Each package creates, migrates and drops its own database on the same server Chosen. Nothing is shared, so nothing needs coordinating A database per test Every test gets a fresh database, usually copied from a migrated template The strongest isolation, needed only when tests inside one package run in parallel (Michael Stapelberg describes this setup)

A database per package is the usual answer to this problem in Go projects that share one Postgres server (a survey of patterns).

internal/dbtest implements it. A suite calls it once, in BeforeSuite:

var _ = BeforeSuite(func(ctx SpecContext) {
    testPool = dbtest.NewPool(ctx, "web")
})

NewPool does the following:

  1. Connects to the server named by TEST_DATABASE_URL, using its postgres maintenance database.
  2. Creates a database with a random name, such as noosphere_test_web_i3eawr5hexkow4f42atmwho53z. The random part keeps two runs of the same package, for example from two terminals, apart as well.
  3. Applies db/migrations to it with goose, so its schema is exactly what the migrations produce.
  4. Returns a connection pool on it.

When the suite ends, the pool is closed and the database is dropped with DROP DATABASE … WITH (FORCE), which also closes any connection a test left open. Creating and migrating a database took 26 to 54 ms in local measurements, once per package.

docs.title: Inside a package: rollback or truncate
docs.text:
Tests inside one Ginkgo suite run one after another, so they only need to clean up after each other. How depends on who commits.

Database tests (internal/db) call the code directly. Each test begins a transaction, runs everything inside it, and rolls it back at the end, so nothing is ever committed. When the code under test starts its own transaction, as sign-up does, it calls Begin on the test's transaction and gets a savepoint instead, which commits or rolls back inside the test's transaction.

Handler tests (internal/web) cannot work that way. The server takes the real connection pool, as it does in production, so its writes are committed. Changing the server to accept a test transaction instead would shape production code around the tests, so the tests adapt: each one starts by emptying every table except goose_db_version, which records the applied migrations:

TRUNCATE identities, identity_credentials, identity_credential_identifiers, registration_flows, sessions

The list of tables is read from pg_tables, so a table added by a new migration is included automatically. The tables are emptied at the start of each test rather than at the end, so a test always begins clean even if the previous run crashed halfway.

docs.title: How others do it
docs.text:
The same two ideas, a separate database where code runs in parallel and rollback or truncation inside it, appear across frameworks and projects:

Who What they do Django TestCase wraps each test in a transaction that is rolled back; TransactionTestCase, for code that commits, "resets the database after the test runs by truncating all tables". With --parallel, "each process gets its own database". Rails Wraps each test in a transaction that is rolled back by default. Parallel workers each get their own database, named test-database-0, test-database-1 and so on. Ory Kratos Its persistence tests run CREATE DATABASE testdb<uuid> on a Postgres started for the tests, then apply the migrations. Most other tests use a fresh SQLite database (pkg/driver.go). Michael Stapelberg One Postgres per go test run, and "a different PostgreSQL database for every test"; creating one takes 5 to 20 ms. Storj Compares a container, a database and a schema per test: about 2 s, about 135 ms and about 25 ms per test in their measurements. Schemas are cheapest but "not as isolated as separate databases". A Go Forum thread The same flaky failures from packages sharing one test database; fixed by creating a database per package in setup and dropping it in teardown. golang/go#61318 An open proposal to run test packages one at a time without also serializing the build, because -p 1 made one project's tests take 8 m 25 s instead of 50 s.

docs.title: What this guarantees
docs.text:
• go test ./..., make test, an editor's test runner and CI all give the same result, whatever runs at the same time. Twenty parallel go test ./... runs and two simultaneous runs in separate terminals all passed.
  • No test data reaches the development database, and no test database outlives its run.
  • Tests inside one package still run one after another. Running a suite's tests in parallel, for example with ginkgo -p, would need a database per test.

docs.title: Ginkgo and Gomega
docs.text:
Specs are written with Ginkgo and Gomega, because nested Describe and It blocks read as statements of behavior. Each package has one standard Go test function that starts its suite, so go test and editors run the specs like any other tests.

Spec names state the rule they prove, scoped exactly as the code or schema scopes it, for example "rejects an identifier already used by another credential of the same type". Test data is written inline and obviously fake (test@example.com, "test-hash"), and the cases are the ones a person would worry about: a different case, surrounding spaces, fullwidth letters, a decomposed é, an invisible character.

make test runs all tests with go test. make test-v runs them through the Ginkgo runner in random order, printing every spec, and accepts extra flags such as ARGS='--focus CreatePasswordIdentity'.

docs.title: Continuous integration
docs.text: Every push to main and every pull request runs the GitHub Actions workflow .github/workflows/ci.yml. It starts a Postgres 18 service with the same credentials as the local database, checks that the code generated by sqlc matches the committed SQL (make generate, then git diff --exit-code), and runs make check.

docs.title: Web
docs.text: Noosphere renders its own pages on the server, in Go. The goal is a small, readable web layer that looks good enough and is easy to test, not a full product UI.

docs.title: Server-rendered pages
docs.text:
The browser asks for a page, and the server returns finished HTML with a form. The form posts back to the same server, which either redirects or renders the page again with errors. Identity providers commonly work this way: their login pages live on their own domain and are rendered by the server, and apps send users there and get them back through redirects.

This keeps the pages that handle passwords simple. Every page works without JavaScript, and nothing is loaded from other domains. A small first-party script adds conveniences on top (see Password field), an approach called progressive enhancement.

The alternative was a JSON API with a separate single-page app, for example in React. That is how many product apps are built, but it means a second codebase, a build step, and cross-origin setup, which this project does not need yet.

docs.title: Flows as data
docs.text: Each request handler first builds the flow as plain data, such as its ID, CSRF token, fields and errors, and only then renders it as HTML. Tests can check that data directly, and a JSON response can later be added from the same data for clients that are not browsers, such as a mobile app.

docs.title: Templates and styling
docs.text:
• Templates use html/template from the standard library. It escapes every value according to where it appears (HTML text, attribute, URL or script), which prevents cross-site scripting by default. templ was the alternative: type-checked, but it adds a code generator.
  • Files (templates and CSS) are compiled into the binary with embed, so tests load exactly what production serves.
  • Styling comes from Pico CSS 2.1.1, in its classless build: plain HTML elements look clean without class names, and invalid fields can be marked with aria-invalid. It is copied into the repository unchanged and served by noosphere itself rather than a CDN, so the password page loads no outside code. A small app.css after it keeps the text at normal size and the page in a narrow column, which suits forms.

docs.title: Routing and middleware
docs.text:
Routes are registered on a chi router, which keeps handlers as plain net/http functions and lists middleware in order:

r := chi.NewRouter()
r.Use(withRequestID)
r.Use(s.withAccessLog)
r.Handle("/static/*", http.FileServerFS(staticFS))
r.Get("/registration", s.getRegistration)

withRequestID gives each request an ID for logging, and withAccessLog writes one log line per request with its status and duration (see Overview). Unknown paths get 404 and wrong methods 405 from the router. A page URL with a trailing slash, such as /registration/, is redirected to the URL without it (middleware.RedirectSlashes), so typed or autocompleted addresses still work.

docs.title: Form fields
docs.text:
The registration form asks for as little as it needs, and says plainly what is optional.

Field Required Stored as Email yes The profile keeps it as typed, without surrounding spaces; the login identifier is normalized with PRECIS First name no As typed, without surrounding spaces Last name no As typed, without surrounding spaces Password yes, 8 to 64 characters Only as an Argon2id hash

The names are optional because many people do not fit a first-and-last-name pattern. The W3C's guidance on personal names around the world says "don't require that people supply a family name": many people in parts of Southern India, Malaysia and Indonesia have only a given name, and Icelanders have no family name. A required field would make them type something false.

Optional fields say so in their label, as in "First name (optional)", and required fields have plain labels. This follows the GOV.UK Design System: "add '(optional)' to the labels of optional fields" and "never mark mandatory fields with asterisks". The word is part of the label, so screen readers read it out with the field, and nobody has to look up what a symbol means.

A password must be 8 to 64 characters long, counted after normalization with each Unicode code point as one character, so an emoji or an accented letter counts once however it was typed. These limits follow NIST SP 800-63B-4 (section 3.1.1.2): 8 is its minimum for a password used together with a second factor, and verifiers should allow at least 64. Used as the only factor, NIST requires 15, so the minimum is expected to rise, or a second factor to arrive. There are no rules about mixing character types, which NIST forbids. The form states the rule under the field ("Use 8 to 64 characters."), and a password outside it gets its own message.

Each field carries the standard autocomplete value (email, given-name, family-name, new-password), so browsers and password managers can fill the form and offer to generate a strong password. When the form is shown again after an error, the typed values come back, but the password field is always empty: the password is never stored in the flow or sent back in a page.

Surrounding spaces are removed on the server. Browsers already strip them from type="email" fields before submitting, but scripts and other clients can send anything, so the server does not rely on the browser.

docs.title: Password field
docs.text:
The password field has an eye icon at its right end, so people can check what they typed before submitting. Its behavior follows the GOV.UK password input component:

  • The password is hidden by default. The icon is a button: an open eye shows the password, a crossed-out eye hides it again. Because it has no visible text, its accessible name ("Show password" or "Hide password") tells screen reader users what it does, and aria-controls points at the field. The icons come from Feather and are drawn inline, so nothing is loaded from elsewhere.
  • The password is hidden again when the form is submitted, so the browser does not keep it as plain text form data.
  • The field has spellcheck="false" and autocapitalize="none", so the browser neither underlines nor changes what is typed once it is visible.

Switching a field between hidden and visible needs JavaScript, so the button is added by static/password-toggle.js, served by noosphere itself. The HTML only marks the field with data-password-toggle; without JavaScript it stays an ordinary password field. The script is a file rather than inline code, so a strict content security policy that allows only the site's own scripts remains possible.

docs.title: Context check
docs.text:
Sign-up refuses a password that is a word from the sign-up itself, with the message "Don't use your email, your name or the site's name as your password." The words are the email, the part of the email before the @, the first and last name if given, and the site's name, noosphere.

The whole password is compared to each word, ignoring case and after the same normalization used for hashing, as NIST SP 800-63B-4 requires: Test@Example.com is refused for the account test@example.com, but test@example.com and a lot more is accepted. Passwords that are only similar to the email are not refused, so the reason for a refusal is always visible to the user (Context-specific passwords).

It is on by default (PASSWORD_CONTEXT_CHECK=true); make run turns it off, like the breached password check, so quick local sign-ups are not refused. The check costs nothing and needs no network, so it runs before the breached password check, and a password it refuses is never sent to the outside service.

docs.title: Breached password check
docs.text:
Sign-up refuses a password that has appeared in a data breach, with the message "This password has appeared in a data breach. Choose a different one." The check asks the Pwned Passwords range API, sending only the first 5 characters of the password's SHA-1 hash and asking for a padded response, so the service learns neither the password nor which one was checked.

It is on by default (PWNED_PASSWORDS_CHECK=true). Local development turns it off in make run, so sign-up works offline and test sign-ups send no requests to an outside service. When it is on:

  • It runs only for a password that already passed the length and character rules, so invalid input never causes a request.
  • It fails open: if the service answers with an error or takes longer than PWNED_PASSWORDS_TIMEOUT (2 seconds by default), the password is accepted and a warning is logged. Sign-up never depends on a service outside noosphere's control.
  • PWNED_PASSWORDS_URL can point at a self-hosted copy of the API instead of the public one.

Tests run against a small fake of the range API, so they do not depend on the internet.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Errors fall into two kinds, and each is always handled the same way:

Kind Examples Response The user can fix it email already registered, invalid email, empty password The form again, with what the user typed (never the password) and a message under each invalid field The form cannot continue CSRF check failed, cookies blocked (403), database unavailable (500) An error page in the site layout, with a link to start again

A form error is saved in the flow's state (the typed values and one message per field), and the browser is redirected back to the form, which renders from the flow. So every page a user sees comes from a GET, and refreshing it never resubmits the form. The invalid field is marked with aria-invalid="true" and linked to its message with aria-describedby, which screen readers announce and Pico styles in red. Checks that cost nothing run first and report together, so a user sees every simple mistake at once; the slow password hash and the database's uniqueness check run only after those pass.

The details of a 500 are only logged, never shown. Plain-text http.Error is used in one place: when rendering a page fails, since rendering is then what broke.

docs.title: Cross-origin protection
docs.text:
Every form post, and any other request that could change something, is first checked for where it came from. Browsers label each request with the Sec-Fetch-Site header (Fetch Metadata) (same-origin, same-site, cross-site or none), and older ones with Origin. A post that a browser marks as coming from another site is rejected with the "Request rejected" page and a 403, before the form is even read.

This uses Go's own http.CrossOriginProtection (Go 1.25), which checks Sec-Fetch-Site, "available in all browsers since 2023", and falls back to comparing the Origin header's host with the request's. GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are always allowed, which is why no GET handler may change state. A request with neither header comes from something other than a browser, such as curl, and is allowed; such a client cannot carry a victim's cookies, so it is not a CSRF risk.

It is a second, independent layer in front of the CSRF token: the OWASP CSRF cheat sheet calls Sec-Fetch-Site "the most useful Fetch Metadata header for blocking CSRF-like cross-origin requests" and requires an Origin check as the fallback, which is exactly what the Go middleware does. Rejections are logged as warnings with the request's Sec-Fetch-Site and Origin values.

docs.title: CSRF cookie
docs.text:
Each browser gets one random CSRF token, in an HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax cookie that is Secure outside local development. Over HTTPS the cookie is named __Host-csrf_token: browsers accept the __Host- prefix (Cookie prefixes) only for a Secure cookie with Path=/ and no Domain, so no other subdomain of the site can set or overwrite it, which closes the main weakness OWASP notes for this pattern. Over plain HTTP in local development, where browsers would refuse that prefix, it is named csrf_token. Every flow the browser starts stores a copy, and a form post must carry the same token as both the cookie and the flow. One token per browser, rather than per flow, lets a user have sign-up open in two tabs.

A browser that does not send the cookie back would otherwise get a new flow, and a new cookie, on every request. Instead it gets a 403 page asking it to allow cookies.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Handler tests start the whole server with httptest, routes and middleware included, on the real connection pool and the test database, whose tables are emptied before each test. A client with a cookie jar acts as the browser and does not follow redirects, so each response can be checked: the status code, the redirect target and the flow behind it, cookies, and the important parts of the page. No browser is needed.

docs.title: Reference implementation
docs.text:
Ory Kratos (commit b86338d) is the identity server. It runs the registration flow, checks the input, and stores identities and sessions. The UI is a separate web app that only renders the forms Kratos describes.

  • Kratos (public API): http://127.0.0.1:4433
  • UI: http://127.0.0.1:4455

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Browser opens the sign-up page: GET :4455/registration.
  2. UI has no flow yet, so it redirects the browser to Kratos to start one: GET :4433/self-service/registration/browser.
  3. Kratos creates a registration flow, sets a CSRF cookie, and redirects back to the UI with the flow ID: /registration?flow=<id>.

  4. UI fetches the flow from Kratos (GET /self-service/registration/flows?id=<id>) and shows the profile form. The flow describes the form (server-driven UI, trimmed):

    {
  "id": "faaa3fc0-0203-4085-ac76-3b6ca668908a",
  "type": "browser",
  "state": "choose_method",
  "expires_at": "2026-10-12T01:10:49Z",
  "ui": {
    "action": "http://127.0.0.1:4433/self-service/registration?flow=faaa3fc0-0203-4085-ac76-3b6ca668908a",
    "method": "POST",
    "nodes": [
      { "attributes": { "name": "csrf_token", "type": "hidden", "value": "<token>" } },
      { "attributes": { "name": "traits.email", "type": "email", "required": true } },
      { "attributes": { "name": "traits.name.first", "type": "text" } },
      { "attributes": { "name": "traits.name.last", "type": "text" } },
      { "attributes": { "name": "method", "type": "submit", "value": "profile" } }
    ]
  }
}

  5. Browser submits the profile to Kratos: POST /self-service/registration?flow=<id>.

    Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

csrf_token=<token>
&traits.email=test@test.com
&traits.name.first=Test1
&traits.name.last=Test
&method=profile

  6. Kratos checks the profile, then changes the form stored in the flow for the next screen: the profile fields become hidden and a password field is added. It redirects back to the UI: /registration?flow=<id>. No account is created yet. Answering a form post with a redirect is the Post/Redirect/Get pattern, so a page refresh does not resubmit the form.

  7. UI fetches the flow again and shows the password form. The profile values are now hidden fields:

    "nodes": [
  { "attributes": { "name": "csrf_token", "type": "hidden", "value": "<token>" } },
  { "attributes": { "name": "traits.email", "type": "hidden", "value": "test@test.com" } },
  { "attributes": { "name": "traits.name.first", "type": "hidden", "value": "Test1" } },
  { "attributes": { "name": "traits.name.last", "type": "hidden", "value": "Test" } },
  { "attributes": { "name": "password", "type": "password", "required": true } },
  { "attributes": { "name": "method", "type": "submit", "value": "password" } },
  { "attributes": { "name": "screen", "type": "submit", "value": "previous" } }
]

  8. Browser submits the password to Kratos, with the profile again: POST /self-service/registration?flow=<id>.

    csrf_token=<token>
&traits.email=test@test.com
&traits.name.first=Test1
&traits.name.last=Test
&password=<password>
&method=password

  9. Kratos checks the input, creates the identity and a session, starts email verification, and redirects (303 See Other) to the UI's verification page with the session cookie:

    HTTP/1.1 303 See Other
Location: http://127.0.0.1:4455/verification?flow=2f6c3de3-1d88-4dfd-916b-fedc463f39f7
Set-Cookie: ory_kratos_session=<session>; …

  10. UI shows the verification form. The user is now logged in.

docs.title: Server-driven UI
docs.text:
Kratos decides what the form contains, and the UI only draws it. Each flow carries ui.nodes (UI nodes), a list of fields with name, type, required flag, value and error messages, plus ui.action and ui.method for where to post. The UI loops over the nodes and renders them. It controls only layout and styling.

This keeps the rules in one place. A new trait in the identity schema (a JSON Schema), or a new method such as passkeys, shows up in every UI without UI changes. Web, mobile and single-page apps render the same nodes. Kratos checks every submit against the flow it stored, so a client cannot skip a step. Errors come back as the same flow with messages on the fields. The cost is flexibility: a fully custom sign-up sequence is harder, because Kratos decides the steps.

docs.title: CSRF
docs.text:
Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) is when another site makes the user's browser send a request the user did not intend. Without protection, another site could post a sign-up form to Kratos from the user's browser. The browser would follow the redirect and store the session cookie, so the user would be logged in to an account the attacker created and controls. Anything the user then enters goes into the attacker's account. This is called login CSRF.

To block this, Kratos requires a secret that only the user's browser holds, and checks that every form post carries it. This is the double-submit cookie pattern:

  • Secret. On the first request from a browser with no CSRF cookie (step 3, GET /self-service/registration/browser), Kratos generates a random secret and stores it in an HttpOnly cookie named csrf_token_<hash>. It is one secret per browser, kept across flows.
  • Form field. Whenever Kratos builds a form (step 3, and again in step 6), it puts a copy of the secret in the hidden csrf_token field. The copy is masked with fresh random bytes each time, which is why the field value differs between steps 5 and 8. Masking protects against BREACH, an attack that recovers a secret repeated unchanged in compressed HTTPS responses.
  • Check. On each submit (steps 5 and 8), Kratos unmasks the field and compares it with the cookie. If they don't match, the post is rejected.

Another site can make the browser send the cookie, but the same-origin policy stops it from reading the cookie or the form, so it cannot fill in the field.

API flows for native apps use no cookies, so they skip this check. Instead, Kratos rejects an API flow request that carries cookies or an Origin header, since that means it came from a browser.

docs.title: Have I Been Pwned
docs.text:
Kratos rejects passwords that have already leaked in a data breach, because attackers try those first, for example in credential stuffing. NIST SP 800-63B-4 §3.1.1.2 requires this: a new password SHALL be compared against a blocklist that includes passwords from previous breaches. Kratos asks Have I Been Pwned (HIBP), using its Pwned Passwords API, without ever sending the password: it asks for a bucket of leaked passwords that look alike, then searches the bucket itself.

This runs on the password submit (step 8), after the length check (at least 8 characters) and a check that the password is not too similar to the email (by Levenshtein distance and longest common substring):

  1. Kratos hashes the password with SHA-1. password becomes 5BAA61E4C9B93F3F0682250B6CF8331B7EE68FD8.
  2. It sends only the first 5 characters: GET https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/5BAA6.
  3. HIBP returns every leaked hash starting with that prefix, as suffix and count. For 5BAA6, that was 1,977 lines on 2026-10-11, including 1E4C9B93F3F0682250B6CF8331B7EE68FD8:52372427.
  4. Kratos looks for its own suffix in the list. If the count is above max_breaches (default 0), the password is rejected with an error on the password field.

Hundreds of passwords share each prefix, so HIBP cannot tell which one was checked. This technique is called k-anonymity; Cloudflare describes its design for HIBP. SHA-1 is used only because the HIBP dataset is indexed by it; the stored password is hashed separately with bcrypt. If HIBP is unreachable, Kratos accepts the password (ignore_network_errors defaults to true). This is a fail-open choice: an outage does not block sign-ups, but the leak check is skipped.

docs.title: Flow
docs.text:
A registration flow is one sign-up attempt, stored on the server until it succeeds or expires. It lets the server check that a form post belongs to an attempt it started, that the attempt is still fresh, and what to show next, such as the email typed so far and the errors to fix. A flow holds:

  • an ID, which appears in the URL and names the attempt;
  • a CSRF token, which the form must send back;
  • its state: submitted values (never the password) and errors per field;
  • an expiry time, after which the flow is rejected and the user starts a new one. The first value is 1 hour.

Noosphere renders the form itself, so the whole flow takes three requests to one server:

Request Does GET /registration Creates a flow and redirects to /registration?flow=<id> GET /registration?flow=<id> Loads the flow and renders the form from it POST /registration?flow=<id> Checks the flow and CSRF token, then creates the account and redirects to /registration/complete, or saves the errors into the flow and redirects back to the form

The redirect after creating a flow puts the flow ID in the URL, so a refresh or the back button shows the same attempt instead of starting a new one. Every form post is also answered with a redirect (Post/Redirect/Get), so a refresh never submits the form twice. Once the account is created, the flow is deleted, so its URL starts a new sign-up instead of showing a form that can only fail.

The CSRF token alone is not enough, because an attacker can start a flow of their own and copy its token into a forged form. The token must also be tied to the browser with a cookie, as in the CSRF note above. A flow is shown only to the browser whose cookie matches it; another browser is given a flow of its own. A browser that does not send the cookie back at all gets a 403 page asking it to allow cookies, instead of a new flow on every request.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Five tables in three groups:

  • The person: identities.
  • How they prove it: identity_credentials holds the secret, and identity_credential_identifiers holds what the user types to find it.
  • Short-lived state: registration_flows for a sign-up in progress, and sessions for a logged-in device.
erDiagram
    identities ||--o{ identity_credentials : "proves with"
    identity_credentials ||--|{ identity_credential_identifiers : "found by"
    identities ||--o{ sessions : "logged in as"
  • identities 1:M identity_credentials: an identity has zero or more credentials, at most one per type.
  • identity_credentials 1:M identity_credential_identifiers: a credential has one or more identifiers.
  • identities 1:M sessions: an identity has zero or more sessions, one per logged-in device.
  • registration_flows stands alone: a flow exists before any identity does.

Every table uses a UUIDv7 primary key, generated by PostgreSQL 18 with uuidv7(). The IDs are unguessable but time-ordered, so new rows append to the index like a sequence. IDs are never used as secrets.

All times are timestamptz, so the server's time zone cannot change what is stored.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text: The examples follow Ada, who signs up with Ada@Example.com.

docs.title: identities
docs.text:
One row per person. Everything else points to it.

Column Type Notes id uuid PK traits jsonb Profile: email, first_name, last_name created_at, updated_at timestamptz

Example:

id traits 01a12be9-a598-707b-a6a3-1f96331092cc {"email": "Ada@Example.com", "first_name": "Ada", "last_name": "Lovelace"}

There is deliberately no unique constraint on traits.email. The profile keeps the email as typed. What must be unique is the login identifier, enforced in identity_credential_identifiers.

docs.title: identity_credentials
docs.text:
One row per way the person can prove who they are: password now, passkeys or social sign-in later. A new login method is a new row, not a new column.

Column Type Notes id uuid PK identity_id uuid → identities, cascade delete type text, checked Login method, such as password; later webauthn or oidc config jsonb Method-specific data, such as the password hash created_at, updated_at timestamptz

Example:

id identity_id type config 01a12be9-a599-74c7-b7e6-70439cada89d 01a12be9-a598-707b-a6a3-1f96331092cc password {"hashed_password": "$argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$9AJst65TcxJXHOvNhnFTHg$/OCLUBfIRQJW1kwtkUYp5oMjgSlILZh6aisfi3VihaM"}

Constraints:

  • FOREIGN KEY (identity_id) → identities, cascade delete. A credential must belong to a real identity. A password credential for identity 01a12be8-3280-7c45-81ad-1c992c1aa770, which does not exist, is rejected. Deleting Ada's identity deletes her password credential with it, so no password is left behind for an account that is gone.
  • CHECK (type IN ('password')). Only known methods. A row with type pasword is rejected instead of becoming a credential no login code ever reads.
  • UNIQUE (identity_id, type). At most one credential per method. A second password row for identity 01a12be9-a598-707b-a6a3-1f96331092cc is rejected; otherwise login would not know which of Ada's two hashes to check.
  • UNIQUE (id, type). Needed only for the foreign key from identity_credential_identifiers. Postgres requires a foreign key to point at columns with a unique constraint.

The password hash is stored in PHC string format. The algorithm and its parameters travel with the hash, so they can be raised later and old hashes upgraded at the next login. Argon2id is the first choice in the OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet. Noosphere uses the cheat sheet's minimum configuration (19 MiB of memory, 2 iterations, 1 degree of parallelism) with a 16-byte random salt per password. Before hashing, the password is normalized with the PRECIS OpaqueString profile (PRECIS), so the same password typed with a different kind of space or a decomposed accent still matches; case and width are kept, so Secret and secret stay different passwords.

docs.title: identity_credential_identifiers
docs.text:
What the user types to find a credential at login, such as their email. The credential is the lock; the identifier says which lock to try. It is a separate table because one credential can have several identifiers, for example a password usable with either an email or a username.

Column Type Notes id uuid PK credential_id uuid The credential this identifier finds type text Login method of the credential, such as password; part of the unique key identifier text What the user types at login, such as ada@example.com; trimmed and lowercased for emails

Example:

id credential_id type identifier 01a12be9-a59a-715f-9320-76c6be463887 01a12be9-a599-74c7-b7e6-70439cada89d password ada@example.com

Constraints:

  • UNIQUE (type, identifier). One account per login. When someone else signs up with ada@example.com, inserting (password, ada@example.com) fails with Postgres error 23505 (unique_violation). This is what stops duplicate sign-ups. A passkey row (webauthn, ada@example.com) is still allowed, because uniqueness is per method.
  • FOREIGN KEY (credential_id, type) → identity_credentials (id, type), cascade delete. The identifier must point at a real credential of the same method. An identifier with credential 01a12be9-a599-74c7-b7e6-70439cada89d and type oidc is rejected, because that credential's type is password. Deleting the credential deletes its identifier, so the email can be used to sign up again.

type is copied into this table because a unique constraint can only cover columns of one table. The composite foreign key is what keeps the copy honest.

Normalization happens before insert, and the rule depends on the method. For password login, emails are trimmed and then normalized with PRECIS, which lowercases them, maps fullwidth letters and rejects invisible characters. So Ada@Example.com is stored as ada@example.com, and ADA@example.com hits the unique constraint. A CHECK constraint rejects any identifier that is not already lowercase, trimmed, in NFC form and non-empty, in case some code path skips normalization. A social sign-in subject ID is case-sensitive and kept as is.

docs.title: sessions
docs.text:
One row per logged-in device. Logging out one device does not touch the others.

Column Type Notes id uuid PK token_hash bytea, unique SHA-256 of the cookie token identity_id uuid → identities, cascade delete Indexed active boolean Set to false on logout authenticated_at, issued_at, expires_at timestamptz

Example, Ada on her laptop and phone, after logging out the phone:

id token_hash identity_id active expires_at 01a12be9-a59b-7960-b916-09ef91f6ffd0 \xca89d7ee0f5c7bdcf54ef44ed4bd7178bd9b61f830f0955e9d4a6e4f0ff14436 01a12be9-a598-707b-a6a3-1f96331092cc true 2026-10-12 10:00 01a12c1f-2100-7259-8053-8c6eb59da032 \x05942f4bfc35d135c2174cd6cbc0441b8719b2701da3fa984524214527b8d19a 01a12be9-a598-707b-a6a3-1f96331092cc false 2026-10-12 11:00

Constraints:

  • UNIQUE (token_hash). A cookie must lead to exactly one session. A second row with the same hash is rejected, so a lookup by cookie can never return someone else's session.
  • FOREIGN KEY (identity_id) → identities, cascade delete. A session for a missing identity is rejected. Deleting Ada's identity deletes both sessions, which logs her out everywhere.

The cookie carries a random 32-byte token, and the table stores only its hash, so a database leak gives no usable sessions. A fast hash is enough here, unlike for passwords, because the token is fully random and cannot be guessed. See the OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet.

identity_id also needs its own index. Postgres does not index foreign key columns automatically, and without it, listing Ada's sessions or deleting her identity scans the whole table.

docs.title: registration_flows
docs.text:
One row per sign-up attempt. It keeps what the user typed and the errors until they succeed, without creating an account.

Column Type Notes id uuid PK csrf_token text Ties the flow to the browser that started it state jsonb Submitted values (never the password) and errors per field expires_at timestamptz Rejected after this; deleted later created_at, updated_at timestamptz

Example, after Ada's first attempt with a password that is too short:

id state expires_at 01a12be8-3280-760b-a59b-6095af80070a {"values": {"email": "Ada@Example.com", "first_name": "Ada", "last_name": "Lovelace"}, "errors": {"password": "must be at least 8 characters"}} 2026-10-11 10:10

Constraints:

  • NOT NULL on expires_at and csrf_token. Every flow must expire and be tied to a browser. A flow without them is rejected, instead of living forever or being usable from any browser.
  • No foreign key to identities. A flow exists before any identity, and most flows never create one.

docs.title: Sign-up transaction
docs.text:
A successful sign-up creates four rows, and they must either all exist or none of them. So they are written in one transaction:

  1. identities: Ada's profile.

    id traits 01a12be9-a598-707b-a6a3-1f96331092cc {"email": "Ada@Example.com", "first_name": "Ada", "last_name": "Lovelace"}

  2. identity_credentials: her password hash.

    id identity_id type config 01a12be9-a599-74c7-b7e6-70439cada89d 01a12be9-a598-707b-a6a3-1f96331092cc password {"hashed_password": "$argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$9AJst65TcxJXHOvNhnFTHg$/OCLUBfIRQJW1kwtkUYp5oMjgSlILZh6aisfi3VihaM"}

  3. identity_credential_identifiers: her email for login.

    id credential_id type identifier 01a12be9-a59a-715f-9320-76c6be463887 01a12be9-a599-74c7-b7e6-70439cada89d password ada@example.com

  4. sessions: her laptop.

    id token_hash identity_id active expires_at 01a12be9-a59b-7960-b916-09ef91f6ffd0 \xca89d7ee0f5c7bdcf54ef44ed4bd7178bd9b61f830f0955e9d4a6e4f0ff14436 01a12be9-a598-707b-a6a3-1f96331092cc true 2026-10-12 10:00

Suppose the email is already taken. Steps 1 and 2 succeed, then step 3 is rejected by UNIQUE (type, identifier). Without a transaction, Ada's identity and password would stay in the database: an account with a password that nobody can log in to. With a transaction, Postgres undoes steps 1 and 2, and the database looks as if the sign-up never happened.

docs.title: Breached password check
docs.text: A breached password check refuses a new password if it has already appeared in a data breach. It works without sending the password anywhere, using a technique called k-anonymity.

docs.title: What problem it solves
docs.text: Attackers do not guess passwords at random. They start with lists of passwords leaked from other services, because people reuse passwords and pick the same popular ones. A password that has leaked once is among the first an attacker tries, however long or complex it looks. NIST SP 800-63B-4 therefore requires checking new passwords against "passwords obtained from previous breach corpuses".

docs.title: Where it is defined
docs.text:
• Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) runs Pwned Passwords, the most used collection of breached passwords, with a free range API: no API key, and "no rate limit".
  • Cloudflare described the k-anonymity design that lets the API be used without revealing the password.
  • NIST SP 800-63B-4, section 3.1.1.2, requires the check as part of a blocklist.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Looked up on 2026-10-24:

Password First 5 characters of its SHA-1 hash Times seen in breaches password 5BAA6 52,372,427 Tr0ub4dor&3 87457 3,196 correct horse battery staple ABF7A 391 quiet-otter-maps-the-river 99FF8 0

Tr0ub4dor&3 looks strong, with mixed case, digits and a symbol, and a strength estimator rates it highly. It is still refused, because it has leaked thousands of times; it became famous from an xkcd comic, and so did correct horse battery staple.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The server hashes the password with SHA-1. password becomes 5BAA61E4C9B93F3F0682250B6CF8331B7EE68FD8.
  2. It sends only the first 5 characters: GET https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/5BAA6.
  3. HIBP returns every leaked hash starting with that prefix, as the remaining 35 characters and a count. For 5BAA6 that was 1,977 lines, including 1E4C9B93F3F0682250B6CF8331B7EE68FD8:52372427.
  4. The server looks for its own remaining characters in the list.

Hundreds of different passwords share each prefix, so HIBP cannot tell which one was checked. With the request header Add-Padding: true, each response is padded to between 800 and 1,000 records with dummy entries of count 0, so its size reveals nothing either (2,159 lines for 5BAA6 with padding). SHA-1 is used only because the dataset is indexed by it; the stored password is hashed separately with Argon2id.

The check needs the network, so a service has to decide what happens when HIBP cannot be reached: accept the password and log a warning (fail open), or refuse the sign-up until it is back (fail closed).

docs.title: Context-specific passwords
docs.text: A context-specific password check refuses a password that is a word tied to the user or the service: their email address, their username, their name, or the name of the site. These are the first words an attacker who knows the account would try.

docs.title: What problem it solves
docs.text: An attacker going after one account already knows a lot about it: the email address used to log in, often the person's name, and of course the site. People still pick exactly these as passwords, because they are easy to remember. A password like Test@Example.com for the account test@example.com, or Noosphere on noosphere, can be long enough to pass a length rule and absent from breach lists, and still fall on an attacker's first try.

docs.title: Where it is defined
docs.text: NIST SP 800-63B-4, section 3.1.1.2, requires new passwords to be compared against a blocklist that includes "context-specific words, such as the name of the service, the username, and derivatives thereof". It also says how to compare: "the entire password SHALL be subject to comparison, not substrings or words that might be contained therein". When a password is refused, the user has to be told why.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
For a user signing up on noosphere as longname@example.com, with the first name Bartholomew:

Password Result Why LongName@Example.com refused the email, in a different case LongName refused the part of the email before the @ bartholomew refused the first name Noosphere refused the site's name longname@example.com and a lot more accepted it contains the email, but is not the email correct horse battery staple accepted not a context word (though a breached password check would refuse it)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
When the password is submitted, the service builds a short list of words from the form and from itself, and refuses the password if it equals any of them:

  1. Collect the context words: the email, the part of it before the @, the names the user entered, and the service's name.
  2. Normalize the password the same way it will be stored, for example turning a no-break space into a plain space, so a lookalike spelling cannot slip through.
  3. Compare the whole password to each word, ignoring case. Only an exact match is refused.

Comparing whole words, as NIST requires, keeps the rule predictable: a user can always see why a password was refused. Some identity servers go further and refuse passwords that are merely similar to the email, measured by edit distance or by how much of the password is shared with the email. That catches variants like longname@example.com1, but it can also refuse passwords for reasons the user cannot see. Variants of common words are mostly caught by a breached password check anyway.

docs.title: Cookie prefixes
docs.text: Cookie prefixes are special starts of a cookie's name, __Host- and __Secure-, that make the browser enforce rules about how the cookie was set. A cookie named __Host-csrf_token is guaranteed to have been set over HTTPS by the exact host that receives it, and by no other.

docs.title: What problem it solves
docs.text: A server cannot tell from a cookie who set it. Normally a site on one subdomain, say blog.example.com, may set a cookie with Domain=example.com, and the browser then sends that cookie to auth.example.com too. If an attacker controls any subdomain, through a vulnerable app or a forgotten DNS record, they can plant or overwrite cookies for the whole site. This is called cookie tossing. It breaks defenses that trust a cookie's value, such as a CSRF token kept in a cookie or a session cookie the attacker swaps for one of their own.

docs.title: Where it is defined
docs.text:
• The prefixes are specified in the IETF's revision of the cookie standard, RFC 6265bis ("Cookies: HTTP State Management Mechanism").
  • MDN's Set-Cookie reference summarizes the rules and browser behavior.
  • The OWASP CSRF cheat sheet recommends the __Host- prefix for CSRF cookies, since such a cookie "cannot be (over)written from another subdomain".

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Which Set-Cookie headers a browser accepts, from an HTTPS page (examples from MDN):

Set-Cookie header Result Why __Host-ID=123; Secure; Path=/ accepted meets every __Host- rule __Host-id=1; Secure rejected missing Path=/ __Host-id=1; Secure; Path=/; Domain=example.com rejected has a Domain __Secure-ID=123; Secure; Domain=example.com accepted __Secure- only requires Secure __Secure-id=1 rejected missing Secure

noosphere's CSRF cookie over HTTPS:

Set-Cookie: __Host-csrf_token=47ISB3EWWBGSHHZI4RDKWEB3DG; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
When a browser receives a cookie whose name starts with a prefix, it checks the cookie's attributes and drops the cookie if any rule is broken:

Prefix Requires Forbids __Secure- Secure, set from an HTTPS page nothing more __Host- Secure, set from an HTTPS page, Path=/ a Domain attribute

Forbidding Domain is what makes __Host- strong. A cookie without a Domain attribute is host-only: the browser returns it "only to the host that sent it", not to subdomains, and only that host can set it. So blog.example.com cannot set a __Host- cookie that auth.example.com would receive. Requiring Path=/ means the cookie applies to the whole host and cannot be shadowed by another cookie of the same name on a narrower path.

Two newer prefixes, __Http- and __Host-Http-, also require HttpOnly, proving the cookie was set by a server response and not by JavaScript. Browsers that do not support prefixes at all accept prefixed cookies like any other, so the prefix adds protection without breaking anything.

docs.title: Fetch Metadata
docs.text: Fetch Metadata is a set of request headers that browsers add to tell the server where a request came from and why it was made. The most useful one, Sec-Fetch-Site, says whether a request was sent by the same site, a related site, an unrelated site, or directly by the user.

docs.title: What problem it solves
docs.text: In a cross-site request forgery (CSRF) attack, a page on another site makes the user's browser send a request to your site, for example by submitting a hidden form. The browser attaches the user's cookies, so the request looks like the user's own. Before Fetch Metadata, a server could not reliably tell such a request from a genuine one, and had to rely on secret tokens in every form. With Sec-Fetch-Site, the browser itself reports that the form was submitted from another site, and the server can refuse it outright.

docs.title: Where it is defined
docs.text:
• The W3C's Fetch Metadata Request Headers specification defines the headers.
  • MDN lists Sec-Fetch-Site as widely available, "across browsers since March 2023".
  • The OWASP CSRF cheat sheet calls Sec-Fetch-Site "the most useful Fetch Metadata header for blocking CSRF-like cross-origin requests", and requires checking the Origin header as a fallback for older browsers.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A sign-up form at https://auth.example.com/registration, submitted in different ways:

How the form was submitted Sec-Fetch-Site Should the server accept it? The user fills in the form on auth.example.com same-origin yes The user opens a bookmarked URL none yes A page on blog.example.com posts to it same-site no: another origin, even within the same site A page on attacker.example posts to it cross-site no

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The browser computes the value by comparing the page that started the request with the server receiving it:

Value Meaning same-origin same scheme, host and port same-site same site (same registrable domain and scheme), but a different origin, such as another subdomain cross-site an unrelated site none started by the user directly: typing a URL, opening a bookmark

Pages cannot fake it: Sec-Fetch-Site is a forbidden request header, so neither JavaScript nor a form can set or change it. Browsers send it only to trustworthy URLs, meaning HTTPS or localhost.

A server applies a simple policy: allow safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) always, which is why those must never change data; allow other methods only when the value is same-origin or none; reject the rest with 403. When a request has no Sec-Fetch-Site, the server compares the Origin header's host with its own; when it has neither header, it comes from something other than a browser, such as curl, which cannot carry a victim's cookies.

Fetch Metadata does not replace CSRF tokens; it adds a layer that works even if a token check has a bug. In Go, http.CrossOriginProtection (Go 1.25) implements exactly this policy.

docs.title: NIST SP 800-63
docs.text: NIST SP 800-63, the Digital Identity Guidelines, is the US government's standard for how services should sign people up, log them in and trust logins from other systems. It is published by NIST, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, an agency of the US Department of Commerce, and is free to read.

docs.title: What problem it solves
docs.text: Authentication is full of habits that feel secure but are not: forced password changes every 90 days, rules like "one uppercase letter, one digit, one symbol", security questions. Each service used to invent its own policy, and many of those policies pushed people toward weak, predictable passwords. SP 800-63 gives one evidence-based set of rules, with clear levels of strictness, that a service can follow and point to.

docs.title: Where it is defined
docs.text:
The current version is Revision 4, released in final form in July 2025 (pages.nist.gov/800-63-4). It has four volumes:

Volume Covers SP 800-63-4 Overview and assurance levels: how sure a service needs to be about who someone is SP 800-63A-4 Identity proofing and enrollment: checking that a person is who they claim when they sign up SP 800-63B-4 Authentication: passwords, second factors, passkeys, sessions, rate limiting SP 800-63C-4 Federation: one system vouching for a user to another, as in OpenID Connect and SAML

It is mandatory for US federal agencies. Elsewhere it is followed as the reference for good practice: the OWASP cheat sheets and many identity products base their defaults on it.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
What SP 800-63B-4, section 3.1.1.2, says about passwords:

Rule Requirement Minimum length 15 characters when the password is the only factor; 8 when it is used with a second factor Maximum length allow at least 64 characters Counting "Each Unicode code point SHALL be counted as a single character" Character rules "SHALL NOT impose other composition rules (e.g., requiring mixtures of different character types)" Blocklist compare new passwords against "commonly used, expected, or compromised passwords": breached passwords, dictionary words, and context words "such as the name of the service, the username, and derivatives thereof" Expiry "SHALL NOT require subscribers to change passwords periodically", only when there is evidence of compromise Guidance "SHALL offer guidance to the subscriber to help the subscriber choose a strong password" Failed attempts limit consecutive failures to no more than 100 for one authenticator

Several of these reverse older habits: no forced expiry, no composition rules, and a breach check instead.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
SP 800-63 sorts requirements into assurance levels, so a service picks the level that matches its risk instead of applying the strictest rules everywhere. Authentication has three levels (AAL1 to AAL3): AAL1 allows a password alone, AAL2 requires two factors, and AAL3 requires a hardware-backed factor that resists phishing. Each requirement uses the words SHALL (required), SHOULD (recommended) and MAY (allowed), as in the IETF's RFCs.

Noosphere uses volume B for its password rules and will meet volumes A and C again in the journeys on email verification and on signing in with another service.

docs.title: OWASP
docs.text: OWASP, the Open Worldwide Application Security Project, is a nonprofit foundation that publishes free, community-written guidance on building secure software. It started in 2001 and was incorporated as the OWASP Foundation in 2004 (about OWASP).

docs.title: What problem it solves
docs.text: Standards such as NIST SP 800-63 say what a service must achieve, for example "store passwords so a leak does not reveal them". Developers also need to know how: which algorithm, which parameters, which header, which mistakes to avoid. OWASP fills that gap with short, practical guides kept up to date by security practitioners.

docs.title: Where it is defined
docs.text:
OWASP's work is organized as projects. The three most used are:

Project What it is Cheat Sheet Series "a concise collection of high value information on specific application security topics", one page per topic Top 10 the ten most critical security risks to web applications, updated every few years ASVS the Application Security Verification Standard, a checklist of security requirements to build and test against; version 5.0.0 was released on 30 May 2025

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The cheat sheets noosphere follows:

Cheat sheet Used for Password Storage Argon2id with at least 19 MiB of memory, 2 iterations and 1 degree of parallelism (Password hashing) Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention the CSRF token tied to the browser by a cookie Session Management session tokens, stored only as hashes Authentication password length rules and login error messages

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: OWASP is not a standards body in the formal sense: its documents are not binding, and anyone can contribute through its public GitHub repositories. Its value comes from being specific, current and widely reviewed. Where NIST and OWASP overlap, they usually agree, since OWASP's authentication guidance cites NIST; OWASP then adds the concrete settings and examples.

docs.title: Password hashing
docs.text: Password hashing turns a password into a fixed string that can be stored and later used to check the password, without the password itself ever being stored. It uses functions that are deliberately slow and memory-hungry, and today's recommended one is Argon2id.

docs.title: What problem it solves
docs.text:
A service has to check passwords, but storing them is dangerous: databases leak. With plain text, every account is exposed at once, and because people reuse passwords, so are their accounts elsewhere. Storing a fast hash such as SHA-256 is not much better:

  • Graphics cards compute billions of SHA-256 hashes per second, so common passwords are found by trying them all.
  • The same password always gives the same hash, so one precomputed table cracks every user with that password.

A password hash fixes both: each guess costs real time and memory, and a random salt per password makes identical passwords hash differently.

docs.title: Where it is defined
docs.text:
• RFC 9106 (2021) specifies Argon2. Argon2 won the Password Hashing Competition (2013 to 2015), and the RFC says Argon2id must be supported by any implementation.
  • The PHC string format, from the same competition, defines how a hash is written down together with its algorithm, parameters and salt.
  • The OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet gives practical settings: Argon2id with at least 19 MiB of memory, 2 iterations and 1 degree of parallelism; scrypt if Argon2id is not available; bcrypt only for legacy systems.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The password correct horse battery staple, stored three ways:

Stored as Value SHA-256 c4bbcb1fbec99d65bf59d85c8cb62ee2db963f0fe106f483d9afa73bd4e39a8a Argon2id, first time $argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$7vmMsXyFPQgp9vP7ZFhbdg$rGLcsnGSHASwcQy5t0n/1w0iSJZWCbcr/wAwP6Q0vkk Argon2id, second time $argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$390lM5l/35sq3Kg3M+eEhQ$hOQfY9g/8eLsKi7P1kRCdH+/6Kyn1TLpoTOnMTiSoTY

The SHA-256 value is the same for everyone who picks this password, and takes nanoseconds to compute. The two Argon2id values differ because each has its own salt, and each took about 20 ms and 19 MiB of memory to compute.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Argon2id fills a block of memory with values derived from the password and the salt, then reads it back in an order that depends on its contents. An attacker cannot skip the memory or trade it for speed, so the cost of each guess is set by the parameters:

Parameter In the PHC string Meaning Memory m=19456 KiB of memory per hash (19 MiB) Iterations t=2 passes over that memory Parallelism p=1 lanes that can run in parallel

The stored string reads as $algorithm$version$parameters$salt$hash, with the salt and hash in base64. To check a login, the server reads the salt and parameters from the stored string, hashes the typed password the same way, and compares the results in constant time. Because the parameters are stored with each hash, they can be raised as hardware gets faster, and old hashes are upgraded the next time their owner logs in.

Before hashing, the password is normalized with the PRECIS OpaqueString profile (PRECIS), so the same password typed with a different kind of space or a decomposed accent gives the same bytes.

In Go, Argon2id is argon2.IDKey in golang.org/x/crypto/argon2.

docs.title: Password strength estimation
docs.text: Password strength estimation guesses how many attempts an attacker would need to find a password, and shows the result while the user types, usually as a meter. The most used estimator is zxcvbn, created at Dropbox.

docs.title: What problem it solves
docs.text: Older strength meters counted character types: a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter, a digit and a symbol meant "strong". That rewards passwords like Tr0ub4dor&3, which attackers guess easily because people make the same substitutions, and punishes long passphrases of plain words. An estimator that models how attackers actually guess gives users honest feedback, which NIST SP 800-63B-4 asks for: verifiers "SHALL offer guidance to the subscriber to help the subscriber choose a strong password".

docs.title: Where it is defined
docs.text:
• D. L. Wheeler, zxcvbn: Low-Budget Password Strength Estimation, USENIX Security 2016, describes the method and compares it with real guessing attacks.
  • dropbox/zxcvbn is the original JavaScript library; zxcvbn-ts is its maintained TypeScript successor.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
zxcvbn 4.4.2 run on 2026-10-24. The score goes from 0 (too guessable) to 4 (very unguessable):

Password Score Estimated guesses Warning password 0 about 10^0.5 "This is a top-10 common password" qwertyuiop 0 about 10^1.4 "This is a top-100 common password" Tr0ub4dor&3 4 about 10^11 none correct horse battery staple 4 about 10^20.3 none quiet-otter-maps-the-river 4 about 10^21.8 none

The table also shows the limit of estimation: Tr0ub4dor&3 scores 4, yet it appears 3,196 times in breached password lists (Breached password check). An estimator judges how a password is built; only a breach check knows whether it has already leaked. The two complement each other.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
zxcvbn splits the password into the most guessable pieces it can find and adds up their cost:

  • words from dictionaries of common passwords, names and English words, also when written with substitutions like 0 for o;
  • keyboard patterns such as qwerty and asdf;
  • repeats (aaaa), sequences (1234, abcd) and dates.

The estimate is the number of guesses an attacker following the same patterns would need, and the score buckets that number. Because its dictionaries are about 1.5 MB compressed, zxcvbn usually runs in the browser as the user types, rather than on the server.

docs.title: PRECIS
docs.text: PRECIS is an IETF standard for checking whether two pieces of text, such as two usernames, should count as the same. The name stands for Preparation, Enforcement, and Comparison of Internationalized Strings.

docs.title: What problem it solves
docs.text:
Text that looks the same to a person can be different bytes to a computer. Uppercase letters, fullwidth letters typed with an East Asian keyboard, and invisible characters copied along with pasted text all change the bytes but not what a person sees. If a login system compares names byte by byte, three things go wrong:

  • One person can create two accounts with the "same" email.
  • A user who signed up as Test@Example.com can't log in as test@example.com.
  • An attacker can register a copy of someone else's name that looks identical on screen.

docs.title: Where it is defined
docs.text:
• RFC 8264 defines the framework.
  • RFC 8265 applies it to usernames and passwords.
  • RFC 8266 applies it to nicknames (display names).

All three were published in 2017. They replace an older standard, Stringprep (RFC 3454).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
These inputs all look like the same email address. Here is what the PRECIS profile for usernames does with each:

Input Result test@example.com test@example.com Test@Example.com test@example.com ｔｅｓｔ@example.com (fullwidth) test@example.com test@example.com with a zero-width space after test Rejected

The first three become the same string, so they are the same account. The last one contains a character with no legitimate use in a name, so it is refused.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Every string is turned into one standard form before it is stored or compared. A profile lists the steps: map fullwidth characters to normal ones, lowercase or keep case, apply Unicode normalization, then reject the string if any character is not allowed. Two strings are the same when their standard forms are identical.

RFC 8265 defines three profiles:

Profile For Case UsernameCaseMapped Usernames and emails Lowercased UsernameCasePreserved Case-sensitive usernames Kept OpaqueString Passwords Kept

Passwords keep their case, because lowercasing would make Secret and secret the same password.

The same profile has to run at sign-up and at login, or the stored name will never match what the user types. PRECIS also cannot catch letters from different alphabets that look alike, such as the Cyrillic а and the Latin a (RFC 8264, Section 12.5).

In Go, the profiles are in golang.org/x/text/secure/precis.

docs.title: Unicode normalization
docs.text: Unicode normalization is a set of standard rules for rewriting text into one agreed form, so that text which means the same thing is also stored as the same bytes. Unicode defines four of these forms: NFC, NFD, NFKC and NFKD.

docs.title: What problem it solves
docs.text:
Unicode often has more than one way to write the same character. é can be one code point (U+00E9), or the letter e followed by a combining accent (U+0301). Both display as é, but the bytes differ, so a program that compares bytes says they are not equal. Which form arrives depends on the device, the keyboard and the software that produced the text.

Without normalization:

  • The same name typed on two different machines may not match.
  • A search for café may miss a stored café.
  • One person can register the "same" account name twice.

docs.title: Where it is defined
docs.text:
• Unicode Standard Annex #15: Unicode Normalization Forms defines the four forms.
  • RFC 5198 asks internet protocols to exchange text in NFC.
  • PRECIS uses NFC as one step when comparing usernames and passwords.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Input NFC NFKC é as one code point (U+00E9) unchanged unchanged e + combining accent (U+0065 U+0301) é as one code point (U+00E9) é as one code point (U+00E9) ｔｅｓｔ (fullwidth) unchanged test ﬁle (with the ﬁ ligature) unchanged file x² unchanged x2

NFC makes the two spellings of é identical and leaves everything else alone. NFKC goes further and also folds lookalike variants into plain letters and digits.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The four forms come from two choices:

Composed (fewest code points) Decomposed (base letter + marks) Canonical: only characters that are truly the same NFC NFD Compatibility: also variants that look alike NFKC NFKD

Canonical forms never change meaning: the two kinds of é are the same character. Compatibility forms can lose information: x² becomes x2, which is no longer "x squared". This is why NFC is the usual choice, and why PRECIS uses NFC and handles fullwidth letters as a separate step.

Normalization only rewrites characters that Unicode considers equivalent. Invisible characters such as the zero-width space pass through unchanged, and so do letters from different alphabets that merely look alike, such as the Cyrillic а and the Latin a.

In Go, the forms are in golang.org/x/text/unicode/norm. Postgres has normalize(text, NFC) and the IS NFC NORMALIZED test (string functions).
